pos: adj. (of stone, hard as stone; of ground, shallow over rock; rendering Hebrew eben, Greek petrodes)
etymology: Stone + y. Ezekiel's phrase is literally the heart of stone; the parable's is the rocky place, ground with rock a finger's depth beneath it.
biblical_def: God's promise of a new heart is stated as surgery: “A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh” (Eze 36:26; Eze 11:19). In the parable some seed “fell upon stony places, where they had not much earth: and forthwith they sprung up, because they had no deepness of earth” (Mat 13:5), and the Lord explains: “he that received the seed into stony places, the same is he that heareth the word, and anon with joy receiveth it; yet hath he not root in himself, but dureth for a while” (Mat 13:20; Mar 4:16). David: “When their judges are overthrown in stony places, they shall hear my words; for they are sweet” (Psa 141:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines stony as made of stone; abounding with stones; hard, unfeeling, obdurate, as a stony heart.
webster_full: STONY, a. Made of stone; as a stony tower.
2. Consisting of stone; abounding with stone; as stony ground.
3. Hard; unfeeling; obdurate; pitiless; as a stony heart.
scriptures: A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh.
And I will give them one heart, and I will put a new spirit within you; and I will take the stony heart out of their flesh, and will give them an heart of flesh:
Mat 13:5
Some fell upon stony places, where they had not much earth: and forthwith they sprung up, because they had no deepness of earth:
But he that received the seed into stony places, the same is he that heareth the word, and anon with joy receiveth it;
Mar 4:16
And these are they likewise which are sown on stony ground; who, when they have heard the word, immediately receive it with gladness;
When their judges are overthrown in stony places, they shall hear my words; for they are sweet.
corruption_summary: Sinners are told to open their hearts, and Ezekiel says the heart is stone and God removes it.
corruption_paragraphs: The invitation to “open your heart to Jesus” assumes a heart with a hinge. Ezekiel describes a heart of stone, and a stone does not open; it is taken out. Every verb in Ezekiel 36:26 has God for its subject — I will give, I will put, I will take away, I will give — and the sinner is the patient on the table, not the surgeon. This is the doctrine of regeneration, and it is why the Reformed insist that the new birth precedes faith rather than following it: a stony heart cannot believe any more than it can beat. The man who did believe should look at the verse and understand what was done to him while he was under.

The stony-ground hearer is the parable's warning against counting joy as conversion. He hears the word and “anon with joy receiveth it” — the response every evangelist hopes for — and he has no root, and when tribulation or persecution ariseth because of the word, by and by he is offended. The seed sprang up fastest where the rock was nearest the surface, because the warmth had nowhere to go. A profession that comes quickly and gladly is not thereby false, but it is not thereby true either, and the decisionism that reports every stony-ground response as a harvest has confused the sprouting with the crop. The parable's test is not how the seed came up but whether it is still there when the sun is hot.
roots_summary: Hebrew eben (H68), a stone; Greek petrodes (G4075), rock-like, rocky; Hebrew sela (H5553), a crag.
roots_lines: Hebrew leb ha'eben (H3820, H68) — the heart of stone; Ezekiel 11:19, 36:26.
Greek petrodes (G4075) — rocky, stony; Matthew 13:5, 13:20, Mark 4:5, 4:16.
Hebrew sela (H5553) — a cliff, crag; Psalm 141:6, “stony places.”
usage: “I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh” — surgery, not an invitation.
“Received the seed into stony places… anon with joy” — the sprout that is not a crop.
“Where they had not much earth” — the rock a finger's depth down.

pos: v. (past participle of toss: thrown about, agitated; rendering Hebrew sa'ar and na'ar, Greek kludonizomai, rhipizo, basanizo, and cheimazo)
etymology: Middle English tossen, of uncertain origin, perhaps Scandinavian. The New Testament's four Greek words are all pictures of water and weather.
biblical_def: The word belongs to the sea. The disciples' ship was “tossed with waves: for the wind was contrary” (Mat 14:24); Paul's was “exceedingly tossed with a tempest” (Act 27:18). Paul makes it a picture of the immature church: “that we henceforth be no more children, tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine” (Eph 4:14). James makes it the double-minded man at prayer: “he that wavereth is like a wave of the sea driven with the wind and tossed” (Jas 1:6). And God speaks to His people by it: “O thou afflicted, tossed with tempest, and not comforted, behold, I will lay thy stones with fair colours” (Isa 54:11). David: “I am tossed up and down as the locust” (Psa 109:23); Solomon: treasures gotten by lying “are a vanity tossed to and fro” (Pro 21:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines toss as to throw with the hand; to lift with a sudden motion; to agitate; to make restless; to be tossed, to be agitated as by waves.
webster_full: TOSS, v.t. To throw with the hand; particularly, to throw with the palm of the hand upward.
2. To throw with violence.
3. To agitate; to make restless; as, calumny tosses the mind.
4. To keep in play; to tumble over; as, to spend four years in tossing the rules of grammar.
scriptures: Eph 4:14
That we henceforth be no more children, tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the sleight of men, and cunning craftiness, whereby they lie in wait to deceive;
Jas 1:6
But let him ask in faith, nothing wavering. For he that wavereth is like a wave of the sea driven with the wind and tossed.
O thou afflicted, tossed with tempest, and not comforted, behold, I will lay thy stones with fair colours, and lay thy foundations with sapphires.
But the ship was now in the midst of the sea, tossed with waves: for the wind was contrary.
And we being exceedingly tossed with a tempest, the next day they lightened the ship;
Pro 21:6
The getting of treasures by a lying tongue is a vanity tossed to and fro of them that seek death.
corruption_summary: Doctrinal instability is admired as open-mindedness, and Paul calls it childhood and gives the church a ministry to grow out of it.
corruption_paragraphs: Ephesians 4:14 names as a defect what the age names as a virtue. To be tossed to and fro and carried about with every wind of doctrine is, in the modern church, to be on a journey, to be humble about one's certainties, to be always learning; Paul calls it being children, and adds that the winds are blown “by the sleight of men, and cunning craftiness, whereby they lie in wait to deceive.” The remedy is in the verses before: Christ gave pastors and teachers “till we all come in the unity of the faith… unto a perfect man.” Settled doctrine is not the enemy of growth; it is what growth is for. A man who is still tossed after twenty years of preaching has either had no pastors or has refused them.

James 1:6 puts the tossing inside the man. The double-minded asker is a wave — not a rock in the wave but the wave itself — driven and tossed, and James says plainly, “let not that man think that he shall receive any thing of the Lord.” The failure is not too little feeling but two minds, and prayer offered from two minds is offered to no one in particular. Isaiah 54:11 is the other side of every sea-verse in the Bible: the One who lets His people be tossed with tempest is the One who speaks to them in it, and the promise that follows is a city built of sapphires.
roots_summary: Hebrew sa'ar (H5590), to storm, be tempest-tossed; na'ar (H5287), to shake off; Greek kludonizomai (G2831), to be tossed by waves; rhipizo (G4494), to fan, toss; basanizo (G928), to distress; cheimazo (G5492), to be storm-driven.
roots_lines: Hebrew sa'ar (H5590) — to be tossed by tempest; Isaiah 54:11; na'ar (H5287), Psalm 109:23; nadaph (H5086), Proverbs 21:6.
Greek kludonizomai (G2831) — to be tossed by waves; Ephesians 4:14 only; rhipizo (G4494), James 1:6 only.
Greek basanizo (G928) — to toss, torment; Matthew 14:24; cheimazo (G5492), Acts 27:18 only.
usage: “Tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine” — childhood, not humility.
“Like a wave of the sea driven with the wind and tossed” — the double-minded at prayer.
“O thou afflicted, tossed with tempest, and not comforted” — and then the sapphires.

pos: adj. (fixed, steady, not yielding; rendering Hebrew kun, yatsuq, and bari, Aramaic taqaph, Greek bebaios)
etymology: Latin firmus, steadfast. Hebrews uses the word of a hope held to the end, and Job of the heart of Leviathan.
biblical_def: The priests bearing the ark “stood firm on dry ground in the midst of Jordan” while all Israel passed over (Jos 3:17). Hebrews: “Christ as a son over his own house; whose house are we, if we hold fast the confidence and the rejoicing of the hope firm unto the end” (Heb 3:6). Of the wicked at ease: “there are no bands in their death: but their strength is firm” (Psa 73:4). Of Leviathan: “His heart is as firm as a stone; yea, as hard as a piece of the nether millstone” (Job 41:24). The presidents of Babylon asked Darius “to establish a royal statute, and to make a firm decree” (Dan 6:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines firm as closely compressed; hard; solid; fixed; steady; constant; not easily moved or shaken.
webster_full: FIRM, a. Properly, closely compressed; compact; hard; solid; as firm flesh; firm muscles.
2. Fixed; steady; constant; stable; unshaken; not easily moved; as a firm believer; a firm friend.
3. Solid; not giving way; opposed to fluid; as firm land.
scriptures: Heb 3:6
But Christ as a son over his own house; whose house are we, if we hold fast the confidence and the rejoicing of the hope firm unto the end.
Jos 3:17

And the priests that bare the ark of the covenant of the LORD stood firm on dry ground in the midst of Jordan, and all the Israelites passed over on dry ground, until all the people were passed clean over Jordan.
His heart is as firm as a stone; yea, as hard as a piece of the nether millstone.
Psa 73:4
For there are no bands in their death: but their strength is firm.
Dan 6:7

All the presidents of the kingdom, the governors, and the princes, the counsellors, and the captains, have consulted together to establish a royal statute, and to make a firm decree, that whosoever shall ask a petition of any God or man for thirty days, save of thee, O king, he shall be cast into the den of lions.
corruption_summary: The if of Hebrews 3:6 is read as making salvation depend on the believer's grip, when it describes the evidence of a house Christ builds and keeps.
corruption_paragraphs: “Whose house are we, if we hold fast… firm unto the end” is the verse the Arminian reads as a condition and the antinomian would rather not read at all. Both miss the shape. The perseverance of the saints is not the doctrine that a Christian will be saved whether or not he perseveres; it is the doctrine that he will persevere, because the One who began the work finishes it, and the holding fast is the evidence by which the house is known. The apostate of chapter 3 — Israel in the wilderness, whose carcases fell — proved by not holding firm that the house was never theirs. Hebrews does not undermine assurance; it locates it. A man knows he is of the house because the hope is still firm in his hand.

Joshua 3:17 shows what firm ground is made of. The priests stood firm in the middle of a river that had stopped flowing, and the ground under them was dry only because the ark was on their shoulders. Firmness in Scripture is always borrowed from what one stands on, which is why Job 41:24 is a warning and not a compliment: Leviathan's heart is firm as a stone, and so is every hardened man's, and Psalm 73 saw the wicked with their strength firm and nearly lost its footing over it — until the sanctuary, and their end.
roots_summary: Hebrew kun (H3559), to be established, fixed; yatsuq (H3332), poured out, cast hard; bari (H1277), fat, robust, firm; Aramaic taqaph (H8631), strong; Greek bebaios (G949), firm, sure.
roots_lines: Hebrew kun, hiphil (H3559) — to stand fixed; Joshua 3:17; yatsuq (H3332), cast hard; Job 41:23–24.
Hebrew bari (H1277) — fat, firm, robust; Psalm 73:4; Aramaic taqaph (H8631), Daniel 6:7.
Greek bebaios (G949) — firm, sure, steadfast; Hebrews 3:6, 3:14, 6:19, 2 Peter 1:10, 1:19.
usage: “If we hold fast… firm unto the end” — the evidence of the house, not its price.
“Stood firm on dry ground in the midst of Jordan” — firmness borrowed from the ark.
“His heart is as firm as a stone” — the wrong kind of firm.

pos: n. (liability to judgment or harm; in the AV chiefly in the phrase in danger of; rendering Greek enochos and kinduneuo)
etymology: Old French dangier, the power of a lord over his subject, from Latin dominium. In the Sermon on the Mount the word keeps its old legal sense: to be in danger of a court is to be within its jurisdiction and liable to its sentence.
biblical_def: The Lord's exposition of the sixth commandment is a scale of danger: “whosoever shall kill shall be in danger of the judgment” (Mat 5:21); “whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment: and whosoever shall say to his brother, Raca, shall be in danger of the council: but whosoever shall say, Thou fool, shall be in danger of hell fire” (Mat 5:22). Of blasphemy against the Holy Ghost: “hath never forgiveness, but is in danger of eternal damnation” (Mar 3:29). Demetrius: “not only this our craft is in danger to be set at nought” (Act 19:27); the town clerk: “we are in danger to be called in question for this day's uproar” (Act 19:40).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines danger as peril; risk; hazard; exposure to injury, loss, pain, or other evil.
webster_full: DANGER, n. Peril; risk; hazard; exposure to injury, loss, pain or other evil.
2. Power to harm; jurisdiction; as, to be within one's danger.
scriptures: Mat 5:21
Ye have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not kill; and whosoever shall kill shall be in danger of the judgment:
Mat 5:22

But I say unto you, That whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment: and whosoever shall say to his brother, Raca, shall be in danger of the council: but whosoever shall say, Thou fool, shall be in danger of hell fire.
Mar 3:29
But he that shall blaspheme against the Holy Ghost hath never forgiveness, but is in danger of eternal damnation:

So that not only this our craft is in danger to be set at nought; but also that the temple of the great goddess Diana should be despised, and her magnificence should be destroyed, whom all Asia and the world worshippeth.
For we are in danger to be called in question for this day's uproar, there being no cause whereby we may give an account of this concourse.
corruption_summary: Anger is ranked among the small sins, and the Lord put it under the same court as murder.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 5:22 is the Lord's own commentary on Thou shalt not kill, and He does not lower the penalty as He widens the crime. The man who kills is in danger of the judgment; the man who is angry without cause is in danger of the same judgment, and the man who calls his brother a fool is in danger of hell fire. Modern casuistry has a category of respectable sins — anger, contempt, the sharp word — and the Sermon on the Mount abolishes the category. The word danger keeps its old legal weight here: to be in danger of a court is to be under its power and awaiting its sentence, and the court in the last clause is Gehenna.

Mark 3:29 has frightened more tender consciences than any verse in the Gospels, and it was spoken to scribes who had just attributed the Spirit's works to Beelzebub with their eyes open. The sin in danger of eternal damnation is a settled, knowing, malicious calling of the Holy Ghost's work devilish, and the anxious Christian who fears he has committed it has, by his fear, demonstrated a heart the scribes did not have. Acts 19 records the world's more honest danger: Demetrius's speech begins with the craft and ends with the goddess, and the order is the true one. Most persecution has been about the craft.
roots_summary: Greek enochos (G1777), held in, liable to, subject to; kinduneuo (G2793), to be in peril.
roots_lines: Greek enochos (G1777) — liable, subject to a court or penalty; Matthew 5:21–22, Mark 3:29, 1 Corinthians 11:27, James 2:10.
Greek kinduneuo (G2793) — to be in danger, run a risk; Acts 19:27, 19:40, Luke 8:23, 1 Corinthians 15:30.
usage: “Whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment” — the same court as murder.
“In danger of eternal damnation” — said to scribes who had chosen their words.
“This our craft is in danger” — the true motive, spoken first.

pos: v. (to strike violently against; to shatter by striking; rendering Hebrew naphats, nagaph, and ratash, Greek proskopto)
etymology: Middle English dasshen, to strike, of Scandinavian origin. In the Psalms it is what the Messiah does to rebel nations and what the angels prevent happening to a foot.
biblical_def: The Father to the Son: “Thou shalt break them with a rod of iron; thou shalt dash them in pieces like a potter's vessel” (Psa 2:9). The angels' charge: “They shall bear thee up in their hands, lest thou dash thy foot against a stone” (Psa 91:12), which the devil quoted to Christ on the pinnacle (Mat 4:6; Luk 4:11). Of Judah: “I will dash them one against another, even the fathers and the sons together, saith the LORD: I will not pity, nor spare, nor have mercy” (Jer 13:14). Elisha wept because Hazael would “dash their children” (2Ki 8:12), and the Medes' bows “shall dash the young men to pieces” (Isa 13:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines dash as to strike suddenly or violently; to break by collision; to throw with violence.
webster_full: DASH, v.t. To strike suddenly or violently, whether throwing or falling; as, to dash one stone against another.
2. To strike and bruise or break; to break by collision.
3. To throw water suddenly, in separate portions.
4. To sprinkle; to confound; to abash; to depress.
scriptures: Psa 2:9
Thou shalt break them with a rod of iron; thou shalt dash them in pieces like a potter's vessel.
They shall bear thee up in their hands, lest thou dash thy foot against a stone.
Mat 4:6

And saith unto him, If thou be the Son of God, cast thyself down: for it is written, He shall give his angels charge concerning thee: and in their hands they shall bear thee up, lest at any time thou dash thy foot against a stone.
And I will dash them one against another, even the fathers and the sons together, saith the LORD: I will not pity, nor spare, nor have mercy, but destroy them.

And Hazael said, Why weepeth my lord? And he answered, Because I know the evil that thou wilt do unto the children of Israel: their strong holds wilt thou set on fire, and their young men wilt thou slay with the sword, and wilt dash their children, and rip up their women with child.
corruption_summary: Christ is preached without a rod, and the devil quoted the psalm about the foot with a clause left out.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 2 is quoted three times in Revelation, and each time it is the rod of iron and the dashing of the nations that is quoted (Rev 2:27; 12:5; 19:15). The Christ of the modern pulpit has no rod. He invites, He accompanies, He affirms, and the psalm the apostles prayed in Acts 4 — “Why did the heathen rage?” — ends with kings kissing the Son lest He be angry and they perish from the way. A gospel that cannot say “thou shalt dash them in pieces like a potter's vessel” has no reason left to say “Kiss the Son.” The mercy is offered because the rod is real.

Matthew 4:6 is the devil's exegesis. He quoted Psalm 91:11–12 accurately as far as it went, and omitted “to keep thee in all thy ways” — the clause that made the promise a promise to a man walking in God's ways and not to a man throwing himself off a roof to test it. Every abuse of a promise since has used the same method: the text quoted, the condition dropped. The Lord answered with another text, and the lesson is that Scripture is not safe in the hands of anyone who will not read it whole.
roots_summary: Hebrew naphats (H5310), to shatter, break in pieces; nagaph (H5062), to strike, stumble; ratash (H7376), to dash in pieces; Greek proskopto (G4350), to strike against.
roots_lines: Hebrew naphats (H5310) — to dash in pieces, shatter; Psalm 2:9, Jeremiah 13:14, Judges 7:19.
Hebrew nagaph (H5062) — to strike, stumble; Psalm 91:12; ratash (H7376), 2 Kings 8:12, Isaiah 13:18.
Greek proskopto (G4350) — to strike against, stumble; Matthew 4:6, Luke 4:11, John 11:9–10.
usage: “Thou shalt dash them in pieces like a potter's vessel” — the rod that makes the mercy urgent.
“Lest thou dash thy foot against a stone” — quoted by the devil, minus a clause.
“I will dash them one against another” — judgment told without softening.

pos: v. (held back, checked; rendering Hebrew kala, batsar, atsar, and kahah, Greek katapauo)
etymology: Latin restringere, to bind back. The word is used of rain, of wombs, of a whole rebellious race, and of two sons a father would not check.
biblical_def: God restrained the flood: “the rain from heaven was restrained” (Gen 8:2). He judged Babel because “now nothing will be restrained from them, which they have imagined to do” (Gen 11:6). Sarai said, “the LORD hath restrained me from bearing” (Gen 16:2). Moses had to stop the offerings for the tabernacle: “the people were restrained from bringing” (Exo 36:6). And of Eli: “I will judge his house for ever for the iniquity which he knoweth; because his sons made themselves vile, and he restrained them not” (1Sa 3:13). Isaiah asks of God's mercies, “are they restrained?” (Isa 63:15). At Lystra Paul and Barnabas “scarce restrained” the people from sacrificing to them (Act 14:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines restrain as to hold back; to check; to hold from action; to repress; to hinder from motion or action.
webster_full: RESTRAIN, v.t. To hold back; to check; to hold from action, proceeding or advancing, either by physical or moral force.
2. To repress; to keep in awe; as, to restrain offenders.
3. To limit; to confine.
4. To withhold; to forbear.
scriptures: For I have told him that I will judge his house for ever for the iniquity which he knoweth; because his sons made themselves vile, and he restrained them not.
Gen 11:6
And the LORD said, Behold, the people is one, and they have all one language; and this they begin to do: and now nothing will be restrained from them, which they have imagined to do.
Gen 8:2
The fountains also of the deep and the windows of heaven were stopped, and the rain from heaven was restrained;
Gen 16:2

And Sarai said unto Abram, Behold now, the LORD hath restrained me from bearing: I pray thee, go in unto my maid; it may be that I may obtain children by her. And Abram hearkened to the voice of Sarai.
Exo 36:6

And Moses gave commandment, and they caused it to be proclaimed throughout the camp, saying, Let neither man nor woman make any more work for the offering of the sanctuary. So the people were restrained from bringing.
And with these sayings scarce restrained they the people, that they had not done sacrifice unto them.
corruption_summary: Permissive fathers are praised for gentleness, and Eli's house was judged for ever because he restrained his sons not.
corruption_paragraphs: Eli was not a silent father. Second Samuel 2 records that he heard what his sons did and spoke to them — “Why do ye such things?… Nay, my sons; for it is no good report that I hear” — and the sentence on his house names the failure exactly: he restrained them not. He rebuked and did not remove; he spoke and did not act; the priests who lay with the women at the tabernacle door kept their office. The modern father who has “talked to” his children and calls it discipline should read 1 Samuel 3:13 slowly. God did not judge Eli for being harsh. He judged him for being a voice without a hand, and the judgment came on the sons, the father, the ark, and the nation in one afternoon.

Genesis 11:6 is the other face of the word: God restraining what man will not. A united humanity with one language had begun to build, and the LORD's judgment was that nothing would now be restrained from them — that unity in rebellion has no natural limit — so He confused the tongues. The scattering was a restraint, and it was mercy; the world has been kept from the worst of what it could do together by the same hand that stopped the rain in Genesis 8. What theology calls common grace, Genesis calls restraint, and it is the only reason the earth has been habitable since.
roots_summary: Hebrew kala (H3607), to shut up, withhold; batsar (H1219), to cut off, make inaccessible; atsar (H6113), to shut up, restrain; kahah (H3543), to rebuke, restrain; Greek katapauo (G2664), to cause to cease.
roots_lines: Hebrew kala (H3607) — to withhold, shut up; Genesis 8:2, Exodus 36:6, Psalm 40:9, 88:8.
Hebrew batsar (H1219) — to withhold, be inaccessible; Genesis 11:6, Job 42:2; atsar (H6113), Genesis 16:2, 20:18.
Hebrew kahah, piel (H3543) — to rebuke, restrain; 1 Samuel 3:13 only; Greek katapauo (G2664), Acts 14:18.
usage: “His sons made themselves vile, and he restrained them not” — a voice without a hand.
“Now nothing will be restrained from them” — why Babel was scattered.
“The LORD hath restrained me from bearing” — Sarai's right theology and wrong plan.

pos: v. (to lift a burden from; to supply the needy; rendering Hebrew chazaq, ashar, and shub, Greek eparkeo)
etymology: Latin relevare, to lift up again. The Hebrew of Leviticus 25 is to strengthen a man; of Isaiah 1, to set right; of Lamentations, to bring back the soul.
biblical_def: Isaiah's programme of repentance: “Learn to do well; seek judgment, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow” (Isa 1:17). The Law: “if thy brother be waxen poor, and fallen in decay with thee; then thou shalt relieve him: yea, though he be a stranger, or a sojourner; that he may live with thee” (Lev 25:35). Paul on widows: “If any man or woman that believeth have widows, let them relieve them, and let not the church be charged; that it may relieve them that are widows indeed” (1Ti 5:16). Jerusalem fallen: “the comforter that should relieve my soul is far from me” (Lam 1:16); her people “have given their pleasant things for meat to relieve the soul” (Lam 1:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines relieve as to free, wholly or partially, from pain, grief, want, or any thing that is considered an evil; to ease; to alleviate; to succor.
webster_full: RELIEVE, v.t. To free, wholly or partially, from pain, grief, want, anxiety, care, toil, trouble, burden, oppression, or any thing that is considered to be an evil; to ease of any thing that pains the body or distresses the mind.
2. To alleviate or remove; as, to relieve pain or distress.
3. To free from any thing that is burdensome; to ease; to help; to succor.
scriptures: Isa 1:17
Learn to do well; seek judgment, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow.
And if thy brother be waxen poor, and fallen in decay with thee; then thou shalt relieve him: yea, though he be a stranger, or a sojourner; that he may live with thee.
If any man or woman that believeth have widows, let them relieve them, and let not the church be charged; that it may relieve them that are widows indeed.
Lam 1:16
For these things I weep; mine eye, mine eye runneth down with water, because the comforter that should relieve my soul is far from me: my children are desolate, because the enemy prevailed.
Lam 1:11
All her people sigh, they seek bread; they have given their pleasant things for meat to relieve the soul: see, O LORD, and consider; for I am become vile.
corruption_summary: Isaiah 1:17 is taken by one side as religion and by the other as politics, and the verse gives mercy as the fruit of repentance, not a substitute for it.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 1 is a chapter about worship God will not accept — the sacrifices, the new moons, the hands spread out that He hides His eyes from — and verse 17 is what He asks instead: learn to do well, relieve the oppressed. Two errors divide the verse between them. The first keeps the temple and drops the widow, and Isaiah says God hates that worship. The second keeps the widow and drops the temple, and calls Isaiah 1:17 a social programme; but the verse sits between “wash you, make you clean” and “though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow,” and it is the fruit of a washed man, not a replacement for washing. Relieving the oppressed is what repentance does with its hands.

First Timothy 5:16 is the order of relief. The believing family relieves its own widows first, so that the church is not charged and can relieve the widows who have no one. The modern reflex runs the other way — the institution first, the family last — and Paul had already said in verse 8 what he thought of a man who provides not for his own: he hath denied the faith. Charity in Scripture has a shape: the near before the far, the family before the church, the church before the state, and every widow relieved by someone.
roots_summary: Hebrew chazaq, hiphil (H2388), to strengthen, uphold; ashar (H833), to set right, make straight; shub, hiphil (H7725), to bring back, restore; Greek eparkeo (G1884), to ward off, relieve.

Hebrew ashar, piel (H833) — to set right, relieve; Isaiah 1:17; shub, hiphil (H7725), to restore the soul; Lamentations 1:11, 1:16, 1:19.

“Let them relieve them, and let not the church be charged” — the family first.
“The comforter that should relieve my soul is far from me” — Jerusalem in Lamentations.

pos: n. (fame, a great name; rendering Hebrew shem, a name)
etymology: Old French renom, from renomer, to name again. The Hebrew behind every occurrence is simply shem, a name — the same word the builders of Babel wanted to make for themselves.
biblical_def: The giants before the flood were “mighty men which were of old, men of renown” (Gen 6:4). Korah's company were “princes of the assembly, famous in the congregation, men of renown” (Num 16:2). Of Jerusalem: “thy renown went forth among the heathen for thy beauty: for it was perfect through my comeliness, which I had put upon thee” (Eze 16:14) — “But thou didst trust in thine own beauty, and playedst the harlot because of thy renown” (Eze 16:15). Of the coming Shepherd: “I will raise up for them a plant of renown” (Eze 34:29). And Daniel to God: “thou… hast gotten thee renown, as at this day” (Dan 9:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines renown as fame; celebrity; exalted reputation derived from the extensive praise of great achievements or accomplishments.
webster_full: RENOWN, n. Fame; celebrity; exalted reputation derived from the extensive praise of great achievements or accomplishments.
scriptures: Gen 6:4

There were giants in the earth in those days; and also after that, when the sons of God came in unto the daughters of men, and they bare children to them, the same became mighty men which were of old, men of renown.
Num 16:2
And they rose up before Moses, with certain of the children of Israel, two hundred and fifty princes of the assembly, famous in the congregation, men of renown:
And thy renown went forth among the heathen for thy beauty: for it was perfect through my comeliness, which I had put upon thee, saith the Lord GOD.
But thou didst trust in thine own beauty, and playedst the harlot because of thy renown, and pouredst out thy fornications on every one that passed by; his it was.
And I will raise up for them a plant of renown, and they shall be no more consumed with hunger in the land, neither bear the shame of the heathen any more.
Dan 9:15
And now, O Lord our God, that hast brought thy people forth out of the land of Egypt with a mighty hand, and hast gotten thee renown, as at this day; we have sinned, we have done wickedly.
corruption_summary: Fame is treated as a neutral good, and the Bible's first men of renown are the generation the flood drowned.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 6:4 is the first celebrity culture. The mighty men of old, the men of renown, are introduced in the verse before “the wickedness of man was great in the earth,” and the next thing recorded about their world is that God drowned it. The pursuit of a name is the sin of Babel a few chapters later — “let us make us a name” — and the men of renown who rose against Moses in Numbers 16 went down alive into the pit with their fame intact. Scripture is not against greatness; it is against renown sought, and it has noticed that the famous in its pages are mostly on the wrong side of the story.

Ezekiel 16 is the autopsy of a renown that was real. Jerusalem's fame went out among the nations for a beauty God had put upon her — the text is emphatic that it was His comeliness — and the very next verse is the fall: she trusted in her own beauty and played the harlot because of her renown. Gifts produce fame, fame produces trust in the gifts, and the trust is the harlotry. The only safe renown in the chapter is God's: “thou hast gotten thee renown, as at this day,” says Daniel, of the exodus — a name made by delivering a people, not by being admired.
roots_summary: Hebrew shem (H8034), a name, and so reputation, fame, renown.
roots_lines: Hebrew anshei hashem (H582, H8034) — men of the name, men of renown; Genesis 6:4, Numbers 16:2.
Hebrew shem (H8034) — name, renown; Ezekiel 16:14–15, 34:29, 39:13, Daniel 9:15, Genesis 11:4.
usage: “Mighty men which were of old, men of renown” — the generation before the flood.
“Playedst the harlot because of thy renown” — fame as the road to the fall.
“A plant of renown” — the Shepherd God raises up.

pos: n. pl. (those who worship; rendering Hebrew obedim, servants, Greek proskunetes and latreuo)
etymology: From worship, Old English weorthscipe, worth-ship. The Greek noun in John 4:23 occurs nowhere else in the New Testament.
biblical_def: The Lord to the woman at the well: “the hour cometh, and now is, when the true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and in truth: for the Father seeketh such to worship him” (John 4:23). Jehu gathered “all the worshippers of Baal” into the house of Baal (2Ki 10:21), let none of the LORD's servants in among them (2Ki 10:23), and slew them all. Hebrews on the old sacrifices: had they been able to perfect, “would they not have ceased to be offered? because that the worshippers once purged should have had no more conscience of sins” (Heb 10:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines worshipper as one who worships; one who pays divine honors to any being; an adorer.
webster_full: WORSHIPPER, n. One who worships; one who pays divine honors to any being; one who adores.
scriptures: John 4:23
But the hour cometh, and now is, when the true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and in truth: for the Father seeketh such to worship him.
Heb 10:2
For then would they not have ceased to be offered? because that the worshippers once purged should have had no more conscience of sins.

And Jehu sent through all Israel: and all the worshippers of Baal came, so that there was not a man left that came not. And they came into the house of Baal; and the house of Baal was full from one end to another.

And Jehu went, and Jehonadab the son of Rechab, into the house of Baal, and said unto the worshippers of Baal, Search, and look that there be here with you none of the servants of the LORD, but the worshippers of Baal only.

Now therefore call unto me all the prophets of Baal, all his servants, and all his priests; let none be wanting: for I have a great sacrifice to do to Baal; whosoever shall be wanting, he shall not live. But Jehu did it in subtilty, to the intent that he might destroy the worshippers of Baal.
corruption_summary: In spirit is read as emotion and in truth as sincerity, and the Lord meant the Holy Spirit and the Word.
corruption_paragraphs: John 4:23 is the charter of worship and the most misread verse about it. In spirit has come to mean with feeling, spontaneously, without form; in truth has come to mean sincerely. The Lord was answering a question about place — this mountain or Jerusalem — and His answer was that the hour had come when worship is no longer located but constituted: by the Spirit, who gives life, and by the truth, which is the Word (“thy word is truth,” John 17:17). Worship in spirit and truth is worship enlivened by the Holy Ghost and regulated by Scripture, and the Father seeketh such worshippers — the one place in the Gospels where the Father is said to seek anything. The Reformed principle that God is to be worshipped only as He has appointed in His Word is not a restriction on this verse; it is this verse.

Hebrews 10:2 proves the finished sacrifice by the worshippers' conscience. If the old offerings had purged, they would have stopped; that they were repeated every year proved they had not, and the worshippers still had a conscience of sins. The argument cuts against every altar that offers again: a sacrifice that must be repeated is by that fact a sacrifice that has not done its work, and the Mass, offered daily, confesses in its calendar what it denies in its theology. Jehu's worshippers of Baal are the word's grim other use — a full house, vestments issued, and not one man left alive.
roots_summary: Hebrew abad (H5647), to serve, worship; Greek proskunetes (G4353), a worshipper; latreuo (G3000), to serve in worship.
roots_lines: Hebrew obedei habba'al (H5647) — the servants, worshippers of Baal; 2 Kings 10:19–23.
Greek proskunetes (G4353) — a worshipper; John 4:23 only.
Greek latreuo (G3000), participle — those who serve, worshippers; Hebrews 10:2, 9:9.
usage: “The true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and in truth” — enlivened by the Spirit, ruled by the Word.
“The worshippers once purged should have had no more conscience of sins” — a repeated sacrifice is an unfinished one.
“All the worshippers of Baal came” — Jehu's full house.

pos: v. (to perceive by touch; to grope; to experience; rendering Hebrew mashash, yada, and bin, Greek pselaphao)
etymology: Old English fēlan, to touch, perceive. In the Authorized Version the word is nearly always the hand's work — Isaac feeling Jacob, Samson feeling for the pillars, the Athenians feeling after God.
biblical_def: Paul at Athens: God made the nations “that they should seek the Lord, if haply they might feel after him, and find him, though he be not far from every one of us” (Act 17:27). Isaac: “Come near, I pray thee, that I may feel thee, my son, whether thou be my very son Esau or not” (Gen 27:21), after Jacob had feared, “My father peradventure will feel me, and I shall seem to him as a deceiver” (Gen 27:12). Egypt's ninth plague was “darkness over the land of Egypt, even darkness which may be felt” (Exo 10:21). Samson asked to “feel the pillars whereupon the house standeth” (Jdg 16:26). “Whoso keepeth the commandment shall feel no evil thing” (Ecc 8:5). “Before your pots can feel the thorns, he shall take them away as with a whirlwind” (Psa 58:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines feel as to perceive by the touch; to have sensation excited by contact; to try by touch; to be affected by; to experience.
webster_full: FEEL, v.t. To perceive by the touch; to have sensation excited by contact of a thing with the body or limbs.
2. To have the sense of; to suffer or enjoy; as, to feel pain; to feel pleasure.
3. To try; to sound; to search; as, to feel after a thing in the dark.
4. To perceive; to know.
scriptures: That they should seek the Lord, if haply they might feel after him, and find him, though he be not far from every one of us:
And Isaac said unto Jacob, Come near, I pray thee, that I may feel thee, my son, whether thou be my very son Esau or not.
My father peradventure will feel me, and I shall seem to him as a deceiver; and I shall bring a curse upon me, and not a blessing.
And the LORD said unto Moses, Stretch out thine hand toward heaven, that there may be darkness over the land of Egypt, even darkness which may be felt.
Ecc 8:5
Whoso keepeth the commandment shall feel no evil thing: and a wise man's heart discerneth both time and judgment.
Psa 58:9
Before your pots can feel the thorns, he shall take them away as with a whirlwind, both living, and in his wrath.
corruption_summary: Feeling is made the organ of faith, and the one man in Genesis who trusted his hands over his ears blessed the wrong son.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaac's blindness made him rely on touch, and touch deceived him. “The voice is Jacob's voice, but the hands are the hands of Esau” — he had the truth in his ears and overruled it with his fingers, and the blessing went by the goatskin. The modern Christian who tests his standing by what he feels is Isaac at the tent door. Faith cometh by hearing, and the assurance that comes by feeling is exactly as reliable as the hair on Jacob's hands: it was real hair, it was really felt, and it was on the wrong man. The word of God is the voice; the feelings are the gloves.

Acts 17:27 is Paul's diagnosis of natural religion. The nations were set in their times and bounds that they might feel after God — the Greek is the groping of a blind man — and Paul's next clause is the point: though he be not far from every one of us. Men grope for a God who is at their elbow, because the groping is done in the dark of Exodus 10, a darkness that may be felt. Natural theology can reach out; it cannot see. Athens had altars to an unknown God because feeling after Him is the most that feeling can do, and the apostle's sermon ended, as it had to, with a man God raised from the dead.
roots_summary: Hebrew mashash (H4959), to feel, grope; yada (H3045), to know, experience; bin (H995), to perceive; Greek pselaphao (G5584), to handle, grope after.
roots_lines: Hebrew mashash (H4959) — to feel, grope; Genesis 27:12, 27:21–22, Exodus 10:21, Judges 16:26, Deuteronomy 28:29.
Hebrew yada (H3045) — to know, experience; Ecclesiastes 8:5; bin (H995), Psalm 58:9.
Greek pselaphao (G5584) — to touch, grope, feel after; Acts 17:27, Luke 24:39, 1 John 1:1, Hebrews 12:18.
usage: “That I may feel thee, my son” — the hands overruled the voice, and blessed the wrong son.
“If haply they might feel after him… though he be not far from every one of us” — groping at His elbow.
“Darkness which may be felt” — the ninth plague.
